body:
in History |   	October 12th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

In 2002, the retired British sub­ma­rine lieu­tenant-com­man­der turned ama­teur his­to­ri­an Gavin Men­zies cre­at­ed a stir with a book about Chi­nese sea­far­ing in the fif­teenth cen­tu­ry. 1421: The Year Chi­na Dis­cov­ered the World (telling­ly titled 1421: The Year Chi­na Dis­cov­ered Amer­i­ca in the Unit­ed States) began as a glob­al his­to­ry of that year, only com­ing to focus on the claim of the title through the inter­ven­tions of pub­lish­ing-indus­try pro­fes­sion­als. They no doubt sensed a lucra­tive con­tro­ver­sy in the off­ing, and events proved them right. Not only did the book turn best­seller, it also man­aged the rare feat of draw­ing, among oth­er respons­es, a two-hour PBS doc­u­men­tary ded­i­cat­ed to debunk­ing it. Today, 1421 is most char­i­ta­bly remem­bered as a work of his­tor­i­cal fic­tion writ­ten around the idea that, even if Chi­na did­n’t actu­al­ly dis­cov­er the world, would­n’t it be neat if it had?
That ques­tion is hard­ly as friv­o­lous as it may sound. Much of Men­zies’ book has to do with the exploits of Zheng He, a Ming-dynasty admi­ral and diplo­mat whose fleet real­ly did make voy­ages to much of the world, or at least the parts sur­round­ing the Indi­an Ocean. Even if the claim that he beat Christo­pher Colum­bus to the Amer­i­c­as can’t be sup­port­ed, he real­ly did get around, and in seri­ous­ly impres­sive ships at that. In the Hoog video above, you can see Zheng He’s sto­ry told with retro 3D video-game graph­ics suit­able to con­vey the kind of adven­ture his life became. Yet it could hard­ly have begun more humbly: born into a Mus­lim fam­i­ly in the south­ern, Mon­gol-con­trolled Yun­nan province, he was cap­tured by the Ming mil­i­tary and cas­trat­ed in ado­les­cence. Harsh though that sounds, it made him able to accrue a kind of pow­er that could nev­er have been his oth­er­wise.
“The Ming empire was built on eunuchs,” says the video’s nar­ra­tor. “Unlike oth­er impe­r­i­al Chi­nese dynas­ties, the Ming ele­vat­ed cas­trat­ed men beyond what any had known.” Their inabil­i­ty to repro­duce and serve their own blood­line inspired the trust of the rulers: “What they lost in muti­la­tion, they gained in access to pow­er.” Under Zhu Di, known as the Yon­gle Emper­or, Zheng He became “the most pow­er­ful eunuch in the Ming Dynasty.” In order to project his pow­er over­seas, the emper­or decid­ed to con­struct “the great­est fleet the world has ever seen,” con­sist­ing of 300 trans­port ships, 180 war­ships, 240 sup­ply ships, 700 horse ships, and 36 mas­sive “trea­sure ships” that might have been the largest wood­en ves­sels ever to set sail. To lead this “mov­ing empire” with its staff of 27,000 — many of them eunuchs — he knew no one more reli­able than his old friend Zheng He.
This fleet’s expe­di­tions main­tained suf­fi­cient hege­mo­ny to ensure a peri­od of region­al sta­bil­i­ty some call the Pax Ming. At the same time, the civ­il ser­vice grew ever more resent­ful of the priv­i­leged eunuch class, and a light­ning strike on the For­bid­den City in 1421 was tak­en as a sign that the time had come to crit­i­cize their lead­er­ship. It would seem that Zhu Gaochi, the Yon­gle Emper­or’s son, took this crit­i­cism to heart. When he took pow­er as the Hongxi Emper­or after his father died while Zheng He was at sea, he put an end to the cost­ly naval expe­di­tions that could, in the­o­ry, one day have reached the New World. Ques­tions about why Chi­na’s age of mar­itime explo­ration had to end have more recent­ly been joined by oth­ers about whether such a vast fleet real­ly could have sailed, and for that mat­ter, whether the enor­mous trea­sure ships could even have been built in the first place. Chi­na may have done away with the eunuch sys­tem more than a cen­tu­ry ago, but there’s no doubt that its cur­rent lead­er­ship rec­og­nizes the impor­tance of sea pow­er — or that it has its eyes on the heav­ens.
Relat­ed con­tent:

The 500-Year-Old Chi­nese “Bagel” That Helped Win a War
How a 16th-Cen­tu­ry Explorer’s Sail­ing Ship Worked: An Ani­mat­ed Video Takes You on a Com­pre­hen­sive Tour
Watch the First Chi­nese Ani­mat­ed Fea­ture Film, Princess Iron Fan, Made Under the Strains of WWII (1941)
Based in Seoul, Col­in Marshall writes and broad­casts on cities, lan­guage, and cul­ture. He’s the author of the newslet­ter Books on Cities as well as the books 한국 요약 금지 (No Sum­ma­riz­ing Korea) and Kore­an Newtro. Fol­low him on the social net­work for­mer­ly known as Twit­ter at @colinmarshall.

There’s ahead of its time, then there’s Traité des couleurs ser­vant à la pein­ture à l’eau —
body:
in Art |   	October 12th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			
There’s ahead of its time, then there’s Traité des couleurs ser­vant à la pein­ture à l’eau — or, in its orig­i­nal Dutch title, Klaer Ligh­t­ende Spiegel der Ver­fkon­st, a 900-page book of paint col­ors made before any such things were com­mon tools of the artist’s, scientist’s, and indus­tri­al designer’s trade. Author and artist A. Boogert cre­at­ed one, and only one, copy of his extra­or­di­nary man­u­al on col­or mix­ing in 1692. Appear­ing on the thresh­old of mod­ern col­or the­o­ry, and fea­tur­ing over 700 pages of col­or swatch­es, the book draws on Aristotle’s sys­tem of col­or rather than the new under­stand­ing of the col­or spec­trum, ful­ly elab­o­rat­ed by New­ton in his Opticks over a decade lat­er.
It would be anoth­er hun­dred years before a flood tide of col­or books began to make the the­o­ry more prac­ti­cal: from Goethe’s 1810 The­o­ry of Col­ors and Werner’s 1814 Nomen­cla­ture of Colour to the dream of col­or stan­dard­iza­tion real­ized: the Pan­tone com­pa­ny, launched in 1963.
But if A. Boogert had much influ­ence on the the­o­ry or prac­ti­cal appli­ca­tion of col­or in his day, there doesn’t seem to be much evi­dence for it. Of course most of the Dutch mas­ters had died when the book was com­plet­ed, and it seems unlike­ly that those still work­ing in 1692 would have been famil­iar with its sin­gle copy.

Instead, the book was meant to edu­cate water­col­orists, hence its French title, which refers to “water-based paint.” (A lit­er­al trans­la­tion of the Dutch runs some­thing like “clear­ly light­ing mir­ror of the paint­ing art.”) Medieval his­to­ri­an Erik Kwakkel found the book in a French data­base, “and it turns out to be quite spe­cial,” he writes, “because it pro­vides an unusu­al peek into the work­shop of 17th-cen­tu­ry painters and illus­tra­tors.

In over 700 pages of hand­writ­ten Dutch, the author, who iden­ti­fies him­self as A. Boogert, describes how to make water­colour paints. He explains how to mix the colours and how to change their tone by adding ‘one, two or three por­tions of water.’… In the 17th Cen­tu­ry, an age known as the Gold­en Age of Dutch Paint­ing, this man­u­al would have hit the right spot.”

The book is cur­rent­ly housed at Bib­lio­thèque Méjanes in Aix-en-Provence, where you’ll find full-page, zoomable, hi-res­o­lu­tion scans. “Beyond being infor­ma­tion­al, the images from the book are stun­ning and addic­tive flip through,” notes Refinery29. “They resem­ble page after page of Pan­tone col­or chips, except with­out the house­hold name.” One won­ders if “A. Boogert” would have become a house­hold name had his book been print­ed and dis­trib­uted. But his col­or sys­tem was already pass­ing away in the New­ton­ian age of col­or spec­trums and wheels, until paint chips final­ly came back in style. Vis­it the col­or man­u­al online here.

Note: An ear­li­er ver­sion of this post appeared on our site in 2019.
Relat­ed Con­tent: 
Goethe’s Col­or­ful & Abstract Illus­tra­tions for His 1810 Trea­tise, The­o­ry of Col­ors: Scans of the First Edi­tion
Werner’s Nomen­cla­ture of Colour, the 19th-Cen­tu­ry “Col­or Dic­tio­nary” Used by Charles Dar­win (1814)
The Vibrant Col­or Wheels Designed by Goethe, New­ton & Oth­er The­o­rists of Col­or (1665–1810)
Josh Jones is a writer and musi­cian based in Durham, NC.

Daily Newsletter
                The Pulitzer Prize-winning Diné artist on latest projects, art in NYC for Indigenous Peoples’ Day, and a Felix Gonzalez-Torres show misses the mark.
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
        
            It’s a beautiful Monday to celebrate Indigenous Peoples’ Day, no matter what the federal government says. In a conversation with Associate Editor Phillip Pyle, Diné musician Raven Chacon discusses his recent improvised performances at the Park Avenue Armory, the “collision” at the heart of all music, and reclaiming the technologies of colonial violence through sound.Read on for a guide to shows centering Native art around New York City — including Shelley Niro and Sarah Sense, two of my favorite artists — and a critique of a Felix Gonzalez-Torres exhibition that bizarrely glosses over the late artist’s AIDS advocacy and political spirit.—Lakshmi Rivera Amin, associate editor

	
		
			Raven Chacon Sounds the History of the Land
		
	
	
		On Wednesday and Thursday night, sound mixers, synthesizers, pedals, speakers, whistles, a turkey call, and a ceramic horn sat on a table at the center of the Veterans Room in Manhattan’s Park Avenue Armory. Serving as the stage for Raven Chacon’s hour-long improvisation sessions for the Armory’s Artists Studio series, the table also offered audiences the rare opportunity to see the prolific artist at play. | Phillip Pyle
	
	
		Read More

title: The Most Expensive Works by Gustav Klimt Sold at Auction

Skip to main content		
		
	
			
	
									
					
	
	Home
	

				
							
					
	
	ARTnews
	

				
							
					
	
	Market
	

				
						

		
									
	October 12, 2026 5:30am	
					
							
		
			
				

			
			
			
	
			
					Gustav Klimt, Portrait of Elisabeth Lederer, 1914-1916
									Sotheby’s
	


				

	In recent decades, Gustav Klimt has become one of the most sought-after artists on the international art market, with his paintings achieving record-breaking prices at auction. From the gilded elegance of his celebrated portraits to the richly patterned views of Lake Attersee completed during his summer retreats, Klimt’s oeuvre embodies the decorative brilliance and artistic innovation that defined Viennese Modernism. The rarity and enduring appeal of these works among collectors have made them some of the most valuable examples of early 20th-century art ever offered for sale.

	The market for Klimt reached new heights with landmark sales of such works as Lady with a Fan in 2023, Blooming Meadow in 2025, and Portrait of Elisabeth Lederer in 2025, each reaffirming the extraordinary demand for his masterpieces. Today, some rank among the most expensive artworks ever sold at auction, including the 10 paintings discussed below.


			
			
	Landhaus am Attersee (Country House by the Attersee), 1914
			
										
					Image Credit: Sotheby’s.				
					
				

	Landhaus am Attersee (Country House by the Attersee) depicts the forester’s house at the entrance to Austria’s Weißenbach Valley, where Gustav Klimt stayed during his summers on the southern shore of Lake Attersee. In this secluded setting, near members of the Flöge family—including his companion Emilie Flöge—the artist refined his mature approach to landscape painting. With oil on canvas, the artist transformed the humble building and surrounding vegetation into a richly patterned composition of vibrant foliage, vivid color, and mosaic-like brushwork. Unlike his meticulously prepared portraits, Klimt’s landscapes were executed with few preparatory studies, lending them a greater sense of immediacy and spontaneity.

	Created during the final phase of Klimt’s Attersee period, the work reflects his fascination with nature as a space of visual intensity. Offered at Sotheby’s New York on November 5, 2003, with an estimate of $18–25 million, the painting achieved $29.1 million. The result confirmed the growing appreciation of Klimt’s landscapes, now regarded as some of the artist’s most personal and innovative achievements.

		
			
			
	Apple Tree I, 1912
			
										
					Image Credit: Christie’s.				
					
				

	Klimt’s Apple Tree I is a luminous example of his mature landscapes, depicting a single apple tree rising above a dense carpet of flowers and foliage. This oil on canvas is distinguished by its vibrant palette, shimmering brushwork, and richly decorative surface, reflecting Klimt’s interest in nature during his summers at Lake Attersee and the influence of Vincent van Gogh’s expressive approach to color and movement.

	First exhibited at the Große Kunstausstellung in Dresden in 1912, the work demonstrates Klimt’s ability to turn a simple natural motif into a striking decorative composition. Its provenance includes ownership by Adele and Ferdinand Bloch-Bauer and its restitution to their heirs in 2006. Offered at Christie’s New York with an estimate of $15–25 million, Apple Tree I sold for $33 million on November 9 of that same year. The sale underscored the enduring appeal of Klimt’s garden landscapes.

		
			
			
	Portrait of Adele Bloch-Bauer II, 1912
			
										
					Image Credit: Christie’s.				
					
				

	Klimt’s Portrait of Adele Bloch-Bauer II is an oil on canvas depicting the eponymous Viennese socialite and salonnière, who was one of Klimt’s most important patrons and the only sitter to whom he devoted two paintings. The first, Portrait of Adele Bloch-Bauer I (1907), is now held by the Neue Galerie New York. The second, along with works such as Apple Tree I (see above), belonged to the Bloch-Bauer family collection that was looted by Nazi authorities after the annexation of Austria in 1938. After a prolonged legal battle, these paintings were returned in 2006 to Maria Altmann and the other heirs of Ferdinand Bloch-Bauer in a landmark restitution case.

	On November 8 of that year, Portrait of Adele Bloch-Bauer II was sold at Christie’s New York as part of an Impressionist and Modern Art Evening Sale. The painting achieved $87.9 million, setting a new auction record for Klimt at the time. In 2016 the work was sold privately by its owner, Oprah Winfrey, who had purchased it at Christie’s, to an anonymous Chinese buyer for a reported $150 million, making it one of the most significant private art transactions of the decade.

		
			
			
	Birch Forest, 1903
			
										
					Image Credit: Christie’s.				
					
				

	“I get up early in the morning, usually around 6 am, sometimes earlier, sometimes later. If I get up and the weather is fine, I go into the nearby forest. I am painting a small beech grove, mixed with a few conifers,” wrote Klimt in a letter to M. Zimmerman in August 1903. It was during his summers in Litzlberg, on the shores of Lake Attersee, that the artist developed his profound connection with the natural world. In Birch Forest (Buchenwald), he captured a secluded grove with precision. The elegant silver trunks rise like “columns in a cathedral created by nature.” Their intricate patterns contrast with the deep green foliage, creating a richly textured surface.

	Landscape occupied a significant place in Klimt’s mature oeuvre, reflecting his search for harmony and visual rhythm. With each tree trunk bearing its own unique markings, the painting shows extreme attention to detail. Acquired by Adele and Ferdinand Bloch-Bauer and confiscated by Nazi forces, Birch Forest was returned to their heirs in 2006 before appearing at Christie’s New York on two occasions. In November 2006, the lot achieved $40.3 million against an estimate of $20−30 million. Returning to the auction house as part of the Paul G. Allen Collection in 2022, it realized $104.6 million, becoming the most expensive Klimt landscape ever sold at auction at the time.

		
			
			
	Litzlberg am Attersee (Litzlberg on the Attersee), 1914
			
										
					Image Credit: Sotheby’s.				
					
				

	Litzlberg am Attersee depicts the shoreline of Lake Attersee, with houses nestled beneath a densely wooded hillside and a narrow stretch of water in the foreground. Recent scholarship suggests the painting was executed in the second half of 1914. Its vibrant palette, flattened perspective, and densely layered brushwork exemplify Klimt’s decorative approach to landscape. The composition is believed to have drawn in part on a postcard photograph of the lake that the artist sent to his nephew in August 1914.

	Acquired directly from Klimt by Viennese patrons Viktor and Paula Zuckerkandl, the painting later entered the collection of Viktor’s sister, Amalie Redlich, a Jewish collector who was dispossessed following the Nazi annexation of Austria and deported to Łódź in 1941. After decades in the collection of the Museum der Moderne Salzburg, the work was restituted to Redlich’s heir in 2011. Later that year, it sold for $40.4 million at Sotheby’s New York, surpassing its $25–30 million estimate. A portion of the sale proceeds was donated to the Museum der Moderne Salzburg to support an extension named in Redlich’s honor.

		
			
			
	Bauerngarten (Flower Garden), 1907
			
										
					Image Credit: Sotheby’s.				
					
				

	Klimt’s Bauerngarten (Blumengarten) (Flower Garden), one of the artist’s most celebrated landscapes, presents an informal profusion of poppies, daisies, zinnias, and roses arranged into a riot of color and pattern. This oil on canvas gives a sense of Klimt’s summers at Lake Attersee and of his evolving approach to landscape, rooted in the symbolic ambitions of the Viennese avant-garde. Painted in the garden of the Mayr-Hof, his summer retreat in Litzlberg, the work shows how the natural and decorative worlds converged under his brush.

	First exhibited at the Kunstschau in Vienna in 1908, the painting attracted attention for its innovative composition and almost mystical treatment of nature. Offered at Sotheby’s London in 2017 with an estimate in excess of $45 million, Bauerngarten sold for approximately $59.3 million, becoming the most expensive Klimt landscape ever sold at auction at the time. The sale underscored the rarity of major Klimt landscapes appearing on the market, with many works of this caliber held in museum collections.

		
			
			
	Portrait of Fräulein Lieser, 1918
			
										
					Image Credit: Wikimedia Commons.				
					
				

	A young woman clad in a flower-patterned cape sits in a frontal pose against a vivid red background. Her face is rendered with delicate, precise details that contrast with the looser, more expressive brushwork characteristic of Klimt’s late style. The identity of the sitter remains uncertain. Earlier catalogues identified her as Margarethe Constance Lieser (1899−1965), while more recent research has suggested that she may have been either Helene Lieser (1898−1962) or Annie Lieser (1901−1972), daughters of the Viennese patrons Henriette and Justus Lieser. Klimt began working on the portrait in 1917, with the model visiting his studio in Hietzing nine times during April and May of that year. The portrait was unfinished when he died of a stroke on February 6, 1918.

	The painting was known to scholars only through a black-and-white photograph, and its whereabouts remained uncertain for decades before it was discovered in Austrian private hands. On April 24, 2024, it was auctioned by Vienna’s im Kinsky, Austria’s second-largest auction house, recognized for its expertise in Klimt’s works and its experience handling restitution-related art sales. Portrait of Fräulein Lieser sold for approximately $41 million including fees, setting a record as the highest price ever achieved for an artwork at auction in Austria. The sale was conducted on behalf of the owners at the time and the legal successors of the Liester family, following an agreement based on the 1998 Washington Principles. The work was purchased by Patti Wong & Associates for an anonymous buyer.

		
			
			
	Dame mit Fächer (Lady with a Fan), 1917−1918
			
										
					Image Credit: Sotheby’s.				
					
				

	Dame mit Fächer is thought to be the last portrait Klimt worked on before his death in 1918; it was still on the easel in his Vienna studio at the time of his passing. The work represents the culmination of the artist’s late portraiture, combining the human presence of the unidentified sitter with the rich patterns and decorative experimentation that defined his last years. Returning to the square format he first employed in Portrait of Sonja Knips (1898), Klimt placed the figure at the center of the composition and surrounded her with motifs drawn from Asian art, including the phoenix and lotus blossoms. The sitter’s elaborate robe also evokes Klimt’s long-standing interest in textiles and fashion, an area closely connected to his companion Emilie Flöge, an influential Viennese fashion designer.

	At Sotheby’s London in June 2023, Dame mit Fächer carried an estimate of more than £65 million ($80 million) and was backed by a third-party guarantee. The painting was hammered in at $93.5 million, reaching $108.4 million with fees and establishing a new auction record for Klimt. The result surpassed the previous record of $104.6 million held by Birch Forest, highlighting the extraordinary demand for Klimt’s late masterpieces in the international market.

		
			
			
	Blumenwiese (Blooming Meadow), 1908
			
										
					Image Credit: Sotheby’s.				
					
				

	In this painting of the meadows surrounding Lake Attersee, Klimt moves away from a traditional landscape format to offer a dazzling carpet of wildflowers—bellflowers buttercups, daisies, cornflowers, clover, and dandelions—that fills the canvas, Here, the horizonless view, square composition, and flattened pictorial space show the influence of late Claude Monet, Japanese art, and emerging Modernist photography.

	Executed likely in the summer of 1908, Blumenwiese represents a pivotal moment in Klimt’s landscape painting, when he pushed the genre toward greater abstraction. The radical composition was so unconventional that some contemporary critics dismissed Klimt’s style as the work of a “madman.” Its distinguished provenance, including ownership by Austro-Galician painter Broncia Koller-Pinell and her husband, Hugo Koller, further enhances its historical significance. The painting sold at Sotheby’s in 2025 for $86 million (including fees), becoming the second-most expensive Klimt landscape ever auctioned and reaffirming its rarity and enduring appeal among collectors.

		
			
			
	Portrait of Elisabeth Lederer, 1914-1916
			
										
					Image Credit: Sotheby’s.				
					
				

	Portrait of Elisabeth Lederer (1914−16) exemplifies Klimt’s mature portrait style, where realism and decoration meet seamlessly. The subject emerges from an elaborate costume that blurs the boundary between figure and background. Completed after nearly three years of revisions, the painting demonstrates Klimt’s meticulous working process and extraordinary feeling for ornamentation.

	Commissioned by the Lederer family, among Klimt’s most important patrons, the painting is one of only two full-length portraits by the artist remaining in private hands. It survived Nazi confiscation during the Second World War and was restituted in 1948. Its provenance, later including a time in the collection of Leonard A. Lauder, makes it one of Klimt’s most significant surviving mature portraits. Estimated at $150 million, the painting was the centerpiece of Sotheby’s November 2025 sales. After a dramatic 20-minute contest between two telephone bidders, it realized $236.4 million (including fees), eclipsing Klimt’s previous record and becoming the second-most expensive work ever sold at auction, behind Leonardo da Vinci’s Salvator Mundi.
